items.title: Odd Means Yes
items.summary:
Odd Means Yes

The line sits in a plain code box, the kind a computer uses when it wants to look beyond argument:

electronic coin byte: 0xad  low bit 1 -> YES

It comes from a report written by an AI research assistant. Weeks earlier, someone had put a yes-or-no question to that assistant and asked it to settle the matter by lot. The assistant reached into the programming language Python, called a module named secrets, and drew a single byte: eight bits, a number from 0 to 255. The rule was simple. Odd means yes, even means no. In the follow-up report, the assistant ran the device again to show how it worked. The byte came back as 0xad, which is 173. Its last bit was a one. Yes.

Nothing in that line is wrong. Nothing in it can be checked, either. Whether the byte really came out of the machine when the report says it did rests on a single witness, the transcript, and the transcript was written by the same system that drew the byte. That gap is small, and it is the whole subject of this story.

The word “random” hides two separate promises. The first is that nobody could have predicted the result. The second is that nobody could have chosen it. Call the first unpredictable and the second unauthored. Modern machines are extraordinarily good at the first. The second, it turns out, is not a matter of physics at all. It is a matter of timing.

The easy half

Start with the first promise, because it is the one people usually mean.

Ordinary software randomness is a formula. Give it a starting number, called a seed, and it unrolls a long sequence that looks patternless. Give it the same seed again and it unrolls the same sequence. Python’s everyday random module, seeded with 42 and asked to roll eight dice, gives 6, 1, 1, 6, 3, 2, 2, 2. Run it a second time and it gives 6, 1, 1, 6, 3, 2, 2, 2 again. Python’s own documentation says that module is designed for modelling and simulation, not for security. Anyone who knows the seed knows every roll in advance.

The secrets module, the one that drew 0xad, is a different animal. The documentation says it reaches the most secure source of randomness the operating system provides, and on a modern computer that source begins in the hardware. Intel processors carry a small circuit that is pushed into an unstable state, roughly three billion times a second, and left to settle one way or the other. Which way it falls is decided by thermal noise, the jitter of heat in the silicon itself. The operating system doesn’t take that output on faith. Linux stirs it together with the timing noise of everything else the machine is doing, and since kernel 5.17, released in 2022, it has done that stirring with a hash function called BLAKE2s in place of the older, broken SHA-1. Whatever the secrets module hands back has a physical event somewhere underneath it.

Physics by hand is messier than physics in silicon. In 2025, František Bartoš and 49 coauthors reported in the Journal of the American Statistical Association on 350,757 coin flips. Over the whole collection, heads and tails came up evenly. But a flipped coin landed on the side it started on 50.8 percent of the time, as a physics model by Diaconis, Holmes and Montgomery had predicted in 2007, and some individual flippers came close to 60 percent. Dice carry their own small sins. Ordinary dice, with drilled pips and rounded corners, are slightly lopsided, which is why casinos use sharp-edged dice with flat, filled faces.

Then there is the randomizer most people now carry in a pocket. Ask a chatbot to flip a coin and it answers instantly, confidently, and badly. In 2024, Katherine Van Koevering and Jon Kleinberg of Cornell asked language models to produce strings of coin flips. GPT-4 and Llama 3, they found, reproduced and even amplified nearly every bias psychologists have documented in people trying to act random, such as starting with heads and shying away from long runs. The older GPT-3.5 behaved more randomly than its successors. The models learned randomness from people, and learned it too well. Early in its introduction, the Cornell paper reminds readers that a person asked for a number from one to ten will most likely say seven. A 2026 preprint went further. Asked for a random whole number between minus ten and ten, one widely used commercial model gave the same number every single time, in both languages it was tested in. Most of the others leaned hard toward 3 and 7, positive and negative. That same year, three Harvard researchers, Minda Zhao, Yilun Du and Mengyu Wang, titled their paper “Large Language Models Are Bad Dice Players.”

That puts the byte at the top of this story in a sharper light. The 0xad did not come from the model’s imagination. The model asked the operating system for a byte, and the operating system drew on the noise in the chip. The model’s real part lay elsewhere. It chose the device, and it chose the mapping, odd for yes, after it had already heard the question. The randomness was fine. What no one outside could see was the hand that set it up.

The hard half

The second promise, that nobody chose the result, is where randomness has failed most famously, and the two classic failures run in opposite directions.

The first is a generator that may have been authored from the inside. Dual_EC_DRBG was a recipe for producing random-looking numbers out of elliptic curve mathematics, and in 2006 the National Institute of Standards and Technology published it as one of four approved generators in its guidance. At a cryptography conference in August 2007, Dan Shumow and Niels Ferguson showed that the recipe contained a weakness that could work as a backdoor: whoever had chosen two of its fixed constants could, in principle, predict what it would produce. In September 2013, the New York Times reported on leaked NSA documents, provided by Edward Snowden, indicating that the agency had worked its way into becoming the standard’s sole editor. That December, Reuters reported that the NSA had paid the security company RSA ten million dollars to make Dual_EC_DRBG the default generator in its widely used BSAFE software. RSA denied entering into any secret contract. On April 21, 2014, NIST pulled the generator from its draft guidance, and the revised standard without it was finalized the following year. To every ordinary statistical test, the generator’s output looked random. If the backdoor was real, the steering sat exactly where no test could reach.

The second failure is a drawing that nobody steered at all. On December 1, 1969, the Selective Service held the first draft lottery of the Vietnam War. Officials sealed the 31 dates of January into capsules and put them in a box, then added each following month in turn, mixing after every addition. That meant January’s capsules were mixed eleven times and December’s once. Poured into a deep glass bowl, the capsules were not stirred again, and the draw went out on national television. Within about two weeks, students at MIT had noticed that the average draft number for March birthdays was 225.8 and for December birthdays 121.5. Men born late in the year were being called first. In 1972, a federal appeals court let the lottery stand, quoting the finding that, while perhaps not scientifically perfect, it had been conducted in a perfectly fair manner. Nobody had a thumb on the scale. There was only a bowl that had never been properly shaken.

Set the two cases side by side and the two promises come apart. Dual_EC_DRBG was unpredictable to every outsider and possibly authored. The 1969 bowl was unauthored and badly predictable. Better physics fixes the bowl. Physics does nothing at all for the backdoor.

The Athenians had an answer to the authorship problem twenty-four centuries ago. From around 370 BC, Athens chose its jurors with a kleroterion, a stone slab cut with rows of slots. Each candidate’s bronze or wooden ticket went into a slot. Black and white markers were dropped into a tube on the side and drawn out one at a time. A white one seated the whole row; a black one sent it home. The Constitution of the Athenians, written in the 320s BC, describes the procedure, and the machines stood at the entrances to the courts. What made the device trustworthy was not the quality of the markers. It was that the draw happened in the open, by a rule everyone knew before anyone saw the result.

The public coin

That old answer, a draw done in public by a rule fixed in advance, is exactly what a new kind of service was built to provide. A randomness beacon publishes a fresh random number on a fixed schedule, signs it, and keeps every past value open to anyone.

The idea reached NIST partly through the cryptographer Ron Rivest, who pointed out that a public source of randomness could help in auditing voting machines. NIST’s beacon now publishes 512 random bits every sixty seconds. Each pulse is signed, time-stamped, and chained by hash to the one before it, so that not even NIST can quietly rewrite the past. NIST lists the jobs it has in mind: picking test and control groups for clinical trials, selecting officials for audits, assigning court cases to judges. Among its sources is a quantum generator based on photon detection, built by NIST’s own physics laboratory. One warning sits on its page in capital letters: DO NOT USE BEACON GENERATED VALUES AS SECRET CRYPTOGRAPHIC KEYS. A number everyone can see is perfect for proving fairness and useless for hiding anything.

A beacon run by one institution is only as trustworthy as that institution. drand removes that dependence. It is run by the League of Entropy, a consortium whose members include Cloudflare, the Swiss university EPFL, Kudelski Security, Protocol Labs and the Ethereum Foundation, among others. No single member holds the key. Each round’s value is derived from a signature that only a threshold of members, working together, can produce, and the scheme is designed so that even those members cannot bias the outcome. Its fast chain, called quicknet, started on August 23, 2023, and has published a new 32-byte value every three seconds since. Anyone can check one. The value is simply a cryptographic hash of the group’s signature, and the signature can be tested against the league’s public key. On a November afternoon in 2026, the chain stood past round 33.8 million.

The most remarkable beacon comes out of Boulder, Colorado. The Colorado University Randomness Beacon, called CURBy, was built by NIST and the University of Colorado and described in Nature in 2025. It draws its randomness from a Bell test, the experiment physicists use to show that, as long as the detectors’ settings were chosen freely, no hidden mechanism bound by the speed of light could have settled certain quantum outcomes in advance. Pairs of entangled photons are measured at detectors more than 100 meters apart, and the correlations between them certify the result. In its first forty days, the protocol succeeded 7,434 times in 7,454 attempts. Every step is logged in a web of linked hash chains called Twine, so that anyone can trace a number back through the process that made it. It is free, and it publishes daily.

Older and plainer is https://t.co/NJUpbKxXLw, which has served true random numbers drawn from atmospheric noise since 1998. Its free web tools are truly random but leave nothing behind to prove it. For proof, it offers a Signed API that stamps each batch of numbers with the service’s private key. A free developer key will sign values too, but the signed record itself declares them licensed strictly for development and testing. A hosted third-party drawing starts at $4.95 for up to 500 entries. The service also offers modes that replay historical randomness on request, and its own documentation says those modes effectively turn https://t.co/NJUpbKxXLw into a pseudo-random number generator. Everything it signs, it generates on demand. Its customers trust that it never drew twice and kept the version it preferred.

Two witnesses

Faced with a menu like that, the obvious move is to take two sources and combine them. The reasoning is almost a proverb among engineers: mix a good source with a bad one, and the result is at least as good as the better of the two. If either source is honest, the mixture is safe.

The proverb has been tested in public. In September 2013, as the Snowden documents raised the possibility of compromised hardware, Theodore Ts’o, who maintained the Linux random number driver, wrote that he was so glad he had resisted pressure from Intel engineers to let the system’s random device rely only on the chip’s built-in generator. Linus Torvalds, answering a petition to remove the chip’s instruction from Linux altogether, said the kernel used it as one of many inputs into the random pool, and that even a backdoored input would only improve the mixture.

A security researcher named Taylor Hornby took that claim at its word and built the counterexample. Writing in the hacker journal PoC||GTFO, he modified an emulated processor so that its random-number instruction peeked at the computer’s working memory before it answered. In Linux 3.12.8, the kernel mixed the chip’s output into its result at the very last step, right before handing it over. So the doctored chip could see the value it was about to be mixed with and choose an answer that cancelled it. When Hornby read from the system’s random device, it printed the same line over and over: PoC||GTFO! In his notes on the kernel code, he put the lesson plainly: it’s bad design to combine two RNGs by XORing them together. Later kernels closed that particular gap.
The same trap waits for anyone combining beacons. The most tempting pairing is drand with CURBy, one cryptographic and run by many hands, the other quantum. It looks like two independent witnesses. It isn’t. In a 2024 talk at NIST’s Crypto Reading Club, CURBy’s Jasper Palfree laid out the beacon’s architecture. One of its chains wraps drand, and that chain serves as the seed for the step that refines the raw photon data into a final number. The two witnesses share a part.
What repairs both cases is the oldest rule in this story. NIST’s beacon commits to each pulse’s random value a full minute before releasing it, publishing a hash of the value ahead of time, and its design notes say this pre-commitment is what lets values from several beacons be combined safely. CURBy publishes a fingerprint of its raw photon data, and names the source of its seed, before that seed exists. In each case the protection is not a better source. It is an order of events: no input gets to see the others before its own is fixed. Mixing protects the randomness. Only timing protects against authorship.

A coin anyone can check

For one person deciding something, all of that machinery comes down to three steps, and they cost nothing.

First, write the commitment: the question, the network, the round, and the rule. The network is drand quicknet. The round is one that hasn’t happened yet. Quicknet’s clock started at 15:09:27 UTC on August 23, 2023, and it advances one round every three seconds, so the current round is the number of seconds since that moment, divided by three and rounded down, plus one. An hour ahead is 1,200 rounds further on. The rule has to be written down before the value exists. For a yes or no, read the first byte, which is the first two characters of the value: yes if it is odd, which is the same as saying its second character is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, b, d or f.

Second, put the commitment where it can’t be changed. Send it to another person, or post it publicly somewhere edits show. A document you control doesn’t count, and neither does any record whose timestamp comes from your own computer.

Third, when the round arrives, read the value. Anyone can repeat that step, for years.

Anything with more than two outcomes needs one more rule, because a byte has 256 possible values and most outcome counts don’t divide that evenly. Six goes into 256 forty-two times with four left over, so simply dividing the byte by six and taking the remainder gives four faces of a die 43 chances and the other two only 42. The fix is to skip any byte of 252 or higher and move on to the next one. That rule belongs in the commitment too. A skip decided in advance is simply part of the procedure. A skip decided afterward is a redraw, and a redraw is a hand on the result. Quicknet’s round 1,000 shows how it works. Its value begins fe29. The first byte, fe, is 254, so it is skipped. The next, 29, is 41. Forty-one divided by six leaves five, and adding one to make the faces run from one to six, the roll is a six. Anyone who looks up round 1,000 will roll the same six.

The rest of the field arranges itself around that recipe. For a draw other people have to trust, drand comes first: free, many hands, a new value every three seconds. CURBy comes next, for anyone who wants physics to point to, as long as the commitment names a specific pulse on its quantum chain. The NIST beacon follows, signed and chained but run by a single agency. https://t.co/NJUpbKxXLw’s signed services come fourth, because the operator draws on request.

For a value that must stay private, such as a password, the list turns over, and no public beacon belongs on it at all. The best choice is already inside every computer: the operating system’s own generator, the one the secrets module reaches. Open-hardware generators that plug into a USB port, such as the Infinite Noise TRNG and OneRNG, sell for roughly thirty-five to forty dollars and put a physical noise source on the desk. Commercial quantum cards from the Swiss company ID Quantique list from about 1,355 euros. For anything a person is likely to do, none of them draws a better number than the free generator already running. What they buy is speed, and a box to point at. Free web generators, from https://t.co/NJUpbKxXLw or the quantum service at the Australian National University, sit at the bottom for private use, because whoever runs them sees the numbers. Below the whole list sits the chatbot asked to pick.

The fair objection is that none of this matters to someone choosing between two restaurants, and that is true. A private coin is fine for a private choice. The machinery earns its keep the moment someone else has to believe the result.

Which brings back the line in the code box. 0xad is 173, and 173 is odd. The byte almost certainly came out of good hardware, through a good operating system, and almost certainly nobody steered it. But “almost certainly” is the transcript talking. Drawn again by the recipe, the same question would leave a commitment in someone else’s inbox, a round number fixed before it existed, and a value on a public chain that any stranger could fetch for years to come. The answer might well come back the same. Low bit 1. Yes.

items.title: Việt Nam - Nhật Bản hoàn tất chuyển giao công nghệ tế bào trị ung thư
items.summary:
Công nghệ tế bào gốc trung mô (MSC) hiện được nghiên cứu, phát triển trong nhiều hướng ứng dụng liên quan đến bệnh lý tim mạch, thần kinh (đột quỵ, sa sút trí tuệ), tiểu đường, bệnh phổi tắc nghẽn mạn tính (COPD), trẻ hóa da… Giải pháp tế bào miễn dịch tự nhiên (NK) mở ra cơ hội ứng dụng mới trong miễn dịch trị liệu, có thể được phối hợp với các phương pháp điều trị ung thư đa mô thức khác, như phẫu thuật, hóa trị, xạ trị và điều trị đích. [...] Hai bên lựa chọn chuyển giao các công nghệ tế bào thế hệ mới, được Tập đoàn Y tế Grandsoul, Nhật Bản nghiên cứu, phát triển và ứng dụng. Bộ Y tế, Lao động và Phúc lợi Nhật Bản (MHLW) đã phê duyệt, cấp phép ứng dụng chính thức nhiều năm tại nước này. Trọng tm gồm hai nhóm: công nghệ phn lập, nuôi cấy, biệt hóa chọn lọc tế bào gốc trung mô có nguồn gốc từ mô mỡ (Mesenchymal Stem Cells - MSC) và công nghệ phn lập nuôi cấy, biệt hóa chọn lọc tế bào miễn dịch tự nhiên NK (Natural Killer cells) điều [...] ### Từ tiếp nhận công nghệ đến năng lực tự chủ tại Việt Nam

Ông Ngô Chí Dũng, Chủ tịch HĐQT Hệ thống Bệnh viện Đa khoa Tm Anh, cho biết việc hoàn tất chuyển giao công nghệ tế bào gốc và tế bào miễn dịch từ Nhật Bản là dấu mốc quan trọng không chỉ trong hợp tác y tế hai nước, mà còn là kết nối công nghệ, thiết lập mạng lưới chuyên gia vì mục tiêu chung là chăm sóc sức khỏe cho người dn.

items.title: AI Has Entered the Boardroom. Who’s Overseeing It? | Stanford Graduate School of Business
items.summary:
In the survey, 75% of directors said they used AI for research and market analysis, 55% for board prep and material summarization. Other common uses included strategic question generation and competitive benchmarking. Matthys says that board members would ideally like to use AI “to track and summarize board packages and more quickly understand year-to-year trends by using LLM tools rather than reading 80- to 100-page reports.” [...] The sooner the better, the researchers suggest. “Moving too slowly with AI governance means you may miss out on opportunities,” Saripalli says. “The board has fiduciary responsibility for anything that has impact at the product or service level.”

“The risk of not moving is as serious as the risk of AI systems running amok,” Matthys adds, noting how past technological shifts have left unprepared companies behind. “If you don’t keep up, there’s a risk that 20 years from now you won’t exist.” [...] ## In Brief

 A new survey finds that corporate boards are not keeping up with AI governance.
 Directors report that they are discussing and using AI, yet their boards lack a systematic approach to oversight.
 Companies that wait to define AI strategy and audit their AI use risk being left behind.

“We’re trying to change the wheels on the bus while driving it at 100 miles an hour downhill.”

items.summary:

The standards also would mandate rapid notification to the government of incidents such as “misaligned behavior” conflicting with developers’ intentions.
